name: Seekh Kabab
description: Juicy Pakistani beef seekh kababs with herbs and spices, mixed until cohesive, shaped evenly on skewers and grilled until browned and fully cooked.
ingredients: 750 g beef mince with some fat
1 small onion, very finely chopped and excess moisture squeezed out
method: Combine the beef mince, well-squeezed onion, green chillies, coriander, ginger-garlic paste, seekh kabab masala, lemon juice and salt in a large bowl.
Mix and knead the mince for several minutes until it becomes tacky and cohesive enough to hold together. Cover and chill for at least 30 minutes so shaping is easier.
With damp or lightly oiled hands, press the mixture firmly and evenly around skewers. Keep the kababs fairly thin and consistent in thickness, with no loose cracks.
Preheat the grill or barbecue well, then cook over medium-high heat. Turn carefully only after the first side has begun to set, brushing lightly with oil if needed.
Continue cooking until evenly browned and fully cooked in the centre. Use a reliable doneness check for minced meat rather than judging only by the charred exterior.
Rest briefly, slide carefully from the skewers and serve hot with chutney, sliced onion and lemon.
tips: Squeeze excess moisture from the onion so the kababs hold to the skewers.
Do not make the kababs too thick or the outside may brown before the centre cooks.
storage: Cool cooked kababs promptly and refrigerate covered. Reheat only the portion you need until thoroughly hot.
image_alt: Mughlai-style seekh kebabs grilled until browned and served as a minced-meat kebab platter
image_caption: Seekh kebabs grilled until browned; a high-resolution Wikimedia Commons photograph used as a visual reference.
technique: A seekh mixture must be cold, cohesive and not watery. Mix until the mince becomes slightly tacky, chill if it feels soft, then press a thin even layer around each skewer so the centre cooks before the outside dries.
doneness_cues: The mixed mince should hold together when pressed rather than shedding visible water.
Raw kababs should grip the skewer without sliding when it is lifted carefully.
The surface should brown in spots while the centre cooks fully.
A cooked kabab should feel springy and juicy, not wet in the centre or dry and crumbly.
mistakes: Adding wet onion, herbs or marinade liquid without controlling moisture.
Shaping a very thick cylinder that browns outside before the centre cooks.
Handling warm soft mince; chilling makes shaping and skewer adhesion easier.
Turning constantly before the first side has set.
substitutions: If using very lean mince, the kababs may cook drier; choose mince with enough natural fat for a juicy result.
Wooden skewers can be used for oven or grill cooking if soaked as appropriate, but metal skewers conduct heat into the centre more effectively.
Green chilli can be reduced without changing the binding of the mixture.
reheating: Reheat covered over gentle heat or briefly in the oven so the kababs warm through without losing too much moisture. Avoid prolonged high heat.

faqs.question: Why does seekh kabab fall off the skewer?
faqs.answer: The mixture is often too wet, too warm or not mixed enough to become cohesive. Chill it and test a small portion before shaping the full batch.

faqs.question: Should seekh kabab mixture be very soft?
faqs.answer: It should be moist but able to hold a ridge when pressed. If liquid squeezes out, correct the moisture before shaping.

faqs.question: How thick should seekh kababs be?
faqs.answer: Keep the layer fairly even and not excessively thick so the centre cooks by the time the surface browns.
